https://www.politico.eu/article/jordan-b.text: PARIS — French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is taking on more international responsibilities for his party, the National Rally, as part of a push to reassure international markets worried about the cost of Marine Le Pen’s populist platform . An aide to Bardella told reporters that the National Rally president’s Friday speech at the Reform UK party congress in Birmingham and visit to the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy on Saturday are the beginning of a concerted campaign to strategically deploy the 30-year-old. Bardella is also slated to give 10 interviews to international media outlets in the coming days. Advertisement Advertisement “Bardella has always been attached to the international credibility of the National Rally,” said the aide, who was granted anonymity to share details of Bardella’s plans. “He will give great attention to the international press during the campaign.” Since shooting up the National Rally’s ranks in his twenties, Bardella has brought a polished professionalism to a party that long struggled to run a tight ship. He led the party to impressive victories in the 2019 and 2024 European elections and is now the head of the Patriots group in the European Parliament. The party is now more popular than ever, and Le Pen is the front-runner to win next year’s presidential election. But when it looked like an embezzlement conviction would doom Le Pen’s chances at running for the presidency, Bardella, as the National Rally’s presumptive candidate, tried to woo more fiscally conservative voters — including France’s business elite — by flirting with a more market-friendly platform than his mentor. But Bardella has been adjusting to a secondary role since an appeals court cleared a path for Le Pen to run as the party’s presidential nominee — and she has made clear that fiscal discipline won’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. That includes her pledge to lower the retirement age for most workers to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year. Bardella is now eyeing a role similar to the one Giorgia Meloni held before she became Italian prime minister in 2022. Bardella “watched with great interest the campaign of Giorgia Meloni, who flooded the international press to reassure institutions and the financial markets,” the aide said. Advertisement Advertisement The carving up of roles between Bardella and Le Pen also makes sense given Le Pen’s spotty track record of international trips — notably her reported failed attempt to meet U.S. President Donald Trump — and the difficulties in shedding the toxic baggage linked to her name. Her father, party founder Jean-Marie, was notorious for downplaying the Holocaust and was convicted of hate speech multiple times. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty Images Volkswagen (VW) Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030 Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure Patrick Daly Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.30 EDT First published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The car company Volkswagen has announced it will shed 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade after being hit by US tariffs and fierce competition from Chinese rivals. The German manufacturer said management and unions had agreed as part of a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000. The number of car models the Volkswagen group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half, while four production plants in Germany could also be shuttered within the next eight years. “It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” Volkswagen group said in a statement. The company said it had approved a plan that involved “the reduction of about 50,000 jobs”, on top of another 50,000 already agreed. Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northern Germany, as part of a company dialogue about the need to address its financial challenges. At the time, Blume’s restructuring plans, which were rumoured to envisage increasing the reduction in headcount from 50,000 to 100,000, were yet to be approved by the VW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders. But on Thursday, the company, Europe’s largest carmaker, said the board had signed-off on the proposals. “The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board’s future plan presented today,” Blume said. “This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen group.” The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees. Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini. On Thursday, Volkswagen also said that management and unions agreed that the future of four German plants – in Hanover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm – could not be guaranteed into the 2030s. VW has faced increasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe , decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe. The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/what-lies-b.text: The Budapest Times The capital with the eye of an expat An unusual pairing Written by Mary Murphy Two things I’m partial to – statues and wine. When I travel, I’m drawn to sculpture parks and cities with statues. In Paris, for instance, a favourite spot is the Musée Rodin. I thoroughly enjoyed my time wandering the streets of Skopje, Macedonia. And Riga, Latvia, is hard to beat when it comes to imposing statues. Come to think of it, that might also be why I gravitate towards cemeteries. Wine and statues, though, they’re an unusual pairing. Or are they? In Jeruzalem, Slovenia, a while back, we ran into a Hungarian couple who told us what Judit Holp was doing out at Memento Park ( Szoborpark) . It’s a museum I keep going back to, so I was curious. Very curious. For those of you who have yet to discover this magical place, I envy you the experience. I’ve been many times and never tire of it. This open-air museum is where the Communist statuary in Hungary was retired to in the early 1990s. The park officially opened on 29 June 1993, the second anniversary of the withdrawal of the Soviet troops from the country. On the left as you go in is the ticketed exhibition, Statue Park itself. Here, in six oval sections, sit 41 statues and monuments that were rescued from Budapest after the fall of Communism. On the right is Neverwas Square (aka Witness Square), with its replica of Stalin’s boots, a symbol of the country’s 1956 Revolution, when Stalin’s statue was pulled from its pedestal by protestors. On either side of the boots are two wooden buildings, reminiscent of internment camp structures that house exhibition spaces. It’s in one of these that you can watch Gábor Zsigmond Papp’s intriguing documentary – The Life of an Agent – detailing the methods used by the secret police. It’s in Hungarian with English subtitles. I’ve seen it so often I could practically act it out. Holp, a lover of both history and wine, decided that the pairing of wine and statues wasn’t at all unusual. And that it worked. And she was right. One of the city’s best-kept secrets is her wine and history nights. A 16-year veteran of the Park, her affinity with her charges is palpable. Last year, we joined the Up reds, whites! wine tasting, featuring wines and statues from both sides of the Spanish Civil War. Some 30 people, mostly Hungarian, followed dutifully as Holp took us through the colourful history of the war, making links to Hungarian history and the statues now resident in the Memento Park – Statue Park. Yes, my Hungarian leaves a lot to be desired, but Google Translate on speaker helped enormously. We began with a non-alcoholic Sangria at the Pallett Bar, for which Holp later provided the recipe. As we drank, we listened to soldiers’ songs from the Spanish Civil War . Our first statue stop was the monument by Greek-Hungarian sculptor Memos Makris to the 1,200 Hungarian volunteers who fought in the Spanish Civil War . This was originally erected in Néphadsereg tér (today’s Honvéd tér ) in district V. Here, we tasted some Henry Winston vintage cider, a nod to George Orwell and his book, Homage to Catalonia . [Holp is a mine of information; her tours are exceptionally well researched, with something for everyone.] Next, it was over to Viktor Kalló’s Monument to the Martyrs of the Counter-Revolution, where Holp filled us in on war correspondents like Robert Capa and works of art by Picasso, Magritte, and Iche inspired by the bombing of Guernica, one of the key events of the Spanish Civil War. We did the dutiful by sampling some cava while Octavio Vazquez and the Guernica Piano Trio provided the background music. The monument was erected in Köztársaság tér in district VIII in 1963. At the Monument to the Fighters of the Workers’ Movement, first homed in Kun Béla Square in 1967, we sampled a dry Lambrusco before moving on to the statue of Miklós Steinmetz, a Hungarian volunteer in the Spanish Civil War who also joined the Soviet Red Army as a volunteer. He once stood at the southeastern end of Budapest, near Budapest airport. Not much is known about what he got up to in Spain; more is known about his death, while a parliamentarian, during the liberation of Budapest. We remembered him with a Cetus Cuvée from the Neuperger Winery. Ferenc Münnich, a good friend and later executioner of Imre Nagy, also fought in the war defending Madrid. A former resident of Néphadsereg tér (today’s Honvéd tér ), his statue was paired with a Syrah from Marques de Grinon in Madrid. It was getting dark by this stage. The atmosphere, lightened by the spirit of the park and the spirit of the wines, was in equal parts giddying and sobering. Holp is a passionate speaker. You didn’t need to understand the language to feel her passion for her subjects. Some Hungarians in our group recalled times when these very statues occupied parks in the city proper, making it all very real. Our final port of call, Zsigmond Kisfaludi-Strobl’s Liberating Soviet Soldier , warranted another Syrah, this time from France, from Baron Philippe de Rotschild. France was one of the main escape routes for Marxists and Trotskyists on the run from Stalin’s purges who fought in the Spanish Civil War. I hadn’t realised that this was part of the original Liberation Monument on Gellért Hill. Today, the female Liberty Statue still stands, but her sidekick, the soldier holding a Soviet flag, was damaged in 1956 and later retired to Memento Park. Back at the Pallet Bar, we enjoyed a Klostor 2023 Riesling Spätlese while quizzing it up to Spanish disco tunes. Even if we didn’t do so well in the quiz (we came last), it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening. One to be repeated. Their next event (in English) is scheduled for Friday, 2nd October , and focuses on the life of Imre Nagy and the wines he encountered or that originate from locations linked to his career. His life journey spanned the European continent, beginning and ending in Hungary, yet far less is known about the events that took place in between. During this guided tour, you’ll get to sample Hungarian, Italian, and Polish wines. Check the Facebook page to register or email them at info@mementopark.hu to book your place. You’ll receive payment details by reply. This event is organised by the volunteers of the Monumentum Public Benefit Foundation, the association supporting the operations of Memento Park. Accordingly, the Foundation is not selling tickets for the program but is collecting donations. They suggest a donation of approximately 9,500–14,500 HUF per person. It’s worth it, as you get to sample some fine wines, learn something more about Hungarian history, and visit Memento Park. And as we’d say in Ireland, Holp has a heavy hand. She doesn’t skimp on the pours. I can’t recommend the experience enough. Get a bunch of your English-speaking friends together and book your spot. It’s one not to be missed. Mary Murphy helps thought leaders find, shape, and articulate their ideas. Humanist modernity: Stanisława and Maciej Nowicki October 1, 2026–March 27, 2027 Add to Calendar Exhibition opening: October 1, 6–8pm Discussion: October 6, 6–8pm, Nowicki’s Unbuilt Chandigarh: An Ecology of Everyday Life Exhibition tour: October 9, 6–8pm, Join us for an exhibition tour with curator Kacper Kępiński. RSVP Center for Architecture 536 LaGuardia Place New York New York 10012 USA niaiu.pl Instagram / Facebook Presented in collaboration between the National Institute of Architecture and Urban Planning in Poland and The Center for Architecture this exhibition showcases the work of Stanisława Sandecka-Nowicka and Maciej (Matthew) Nowicki, two significant figures in the history of American and Polish architecture. Named for a concept developed in the 1940s by architects Maciej (Matthew) Nowicki and Stanisława Sandecka Nowicka, Humanist modernity explores their vision of modernism as a human-centered approach to design—one concerned with understanding who a building is really for, and how it binds a human being to the space around them. The exhibition follows this idea across their work and asks what their architecture offers us today. The first exhibition to present the Nowickis as equal partners in a shared body of work, it explores a practice that bridges drawing, building, graphics, and structure, across Europe, America, and India. While Nowicki died tragically at age 40 when his plane crashed as he returned from a job site in India, several years later Sandecka-Nowicka went on to become the first woman in the United States to be appointed as a full professor of architecture when she was appointed as such at the University of Pennsylvania in 1963. She taught fundamental design principles until her retirement as Professor Emeritus in 1977 and received the American Institute of Architects medal in 1978 for her lifelong influence on the profession. Humanist modernity opened at the United Nations Headquarters in New York in January 2024, then traveled to Raleigh, North Carolina, the city of the Dorton Arena (2024); to the ZODIAK Warsaw Architecture Pavilion (April to July 2025); to the Museum of Architecture in Wrocław (from March 2026); and to the Government Museum and Art Gallery in Chandigarh (May to July 2026). Its presentation at the Center for Architecture returns the Nowickis to the city where so much of their American story took place. Artists participating in exhibition: Centrala (Małgorzata Kuciewicz and Simone De Iacobis), Alicja Bielawska, Diana Lelonek Curator: Kacper Kępiński / Curatorial collaboration: Karolina Częczek, Grzegorz Piątek. The exhibition is organized by the National Institute of Architecture and Urban Planning, Warsaw, Poland, and co financed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage. Exhibition is supported by The New York State Council on the Arts with the support of the Office of Governor and the New York State Legislature Program is supported by Polish Cultural Institute New York.
